paragraphs: DropEdge trains graph neural networks on altered versions of a graph by randomly removing connections. This exposes the model to different structures and can reduce overfitting to particular edges. The paper asks why this seemingly useful augmentation nevertheless delivers only limited gains in supervised learning.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis that attributes the limitation to a fundamental feature of many graph neural network architectures. Their response is Aggregation Buffer, an additional block of trainable parameters designed around that analysis. The contribution therefore combines an explanation of why edge removal can underperform with an architectural way to address the identified problem.

The authors describe the block as compatible with any graph neural network and report consistent improvements across multiple datasets. They also find that it addresses degree bias and structural disparity, connecting these problems through a common intervention. The findings suggest that making models more robust to graph structure requires attention to their aggregation architecture as well as the structural variations presented during training.
icml-2025-aggregation-buffer-revisiting-.tldr: Aggregation Buffer adds a trainable parameter block to graph neural networks to address architectural limits on DropEdge’s benefits.

paragraphs: Estimating a mean becomes difficult when observations contain adversarial outliers or come from distributions with very heavy tails. This paper studies whether an existing one-dimensional estimator can handle those settings while retaining its already established, constant-factor optimal performance for independent, identically distributed data with finite variance.

The authors prove robustness when an adversary corrupts an η fraction of the data, including under the strong contamination model. For distributions with variance σ², the corruption-related estimation error has the optimal order σ√η. They also establish optimal error up to constants when only a finite moment of order between one and two exists, covering some distributions with infinite variance.

A further result links robustness to neighborhood optimality, a distribution-dependent notion that goes beyond worst-case guarantees. The stated guarantee applies to estimators that are both robust and sub-Gaussian, extending its previously known reach. Finally, the authors establish asymptotic normality and efficiency for the studied estimator. Together, these results support using the same procedure across several distinct statistical regimes without giving up its standard-setting optimality.
icml-2025-all-purpose-mean-estimation-ov.tldr: The paper proves that an already optimal one-dimensional mean estimator also handles adversarial corruption and heavy tails.

paragraphs: Neural scaling laws describe how model performance changes as resources increase. Predicting beyond observed scales can help decide whether additional computation is worthwhile, but a single predicted value leaves uncertainty unresolved. This paper develops a Bayesian approach that aims to provide uncertainty-aware predictions of performance at larger scales.

The method uses a Prior-data Fitted Network, or PFN. The authors construct a prior distribution from which they can sample arbitrarily many synthetic functions resembling real neural scaling laws. Training across these functions lets the network learn the extrapolation task itself, using simulated scaling behavior as preparation for reasoning about actual observed curves.

The authors evaluate the approach on real neural scaling laws against both point-estimation methods and Bayesian alternatives. They report superior performance, especially when observations are scarce, including in Bayesian active learning. This makes the approach relevant to decisions where collecting more scaling measurements is constrained. The stated findings support its potential for more reliable extrapolation that represents uncertainty, rather than providing only an expected outcome from additional resources.
icml-2025-bayesian-neural-scaling-law-ex.tldr: A network trained on synthetic scaling curves improves uncertainty-aware extrapolation, particularly when few real measurements are available.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation updates a trained model using unlabeled data encountered during deployment. In changing environments, those updates can help the model follow a shifting distribution. They also introduce gradient noise through unsupervised learning, which can degrade the weights and make continued adaptation unstable.

The paper introduces a Bayesian framework that represents model weights through distributions. This framework generalizes existing methods that protect weights during adaptation and reveals a shared omission: they do not account for covariance changing over time. That covariance reflects the influence of gradient noise, so its evolution matters for understanding how adaptation affects the model.

The authors derive steady-state adaptation, or SSA, using a stochastic differential equation describing the adaptation process together with online inference. The resulting algorithm adjusts the learning rate using covariance information to balance these dynamics. Across the tested adaptation scenarios, datasets, and architectures, SSA consistently improves existing state-of-the-art methods. The results support treating evolving weight uncertainty as a practical signal for achieving a better balance between stability and responsiveness.
icml-2025-bayesian-weight-enhancement-wi.tldr: SSA uses changing weight covariance to adjust learning rates and improve test-time adaptation across the evaluated settings.

paragraphs: Macro placement determines where large groups of components sit on a chip, making it an important influence on chip performance. Existing learning-based approaches often use reinforcement learning and require online training for each new circuit. This paper investigates a diffusion model that can produce placements for previously unseen circuits without that circuit-specific training.

The model uses guided sampling to improve placement quality during generation. To make training at scale feasible, the authors design an efficient denoising architecture and an algorithm for producing large synthetic training datasets. Synthetic data generation is a central part of the method because the learned placement behavior must transfer to realistic circuits.

The authors empirically examine dataset-generation choices and identify factors that enable this transfer. Models trained on their synthetic data produce high-quality placements on unseen realistic circuits and achieve competitive results against state-of-the-art placement methods. The contribution connects scalable synthetic training with zero-shot placement, showing that the evaluated circuits can be handled by a pretrained generator while sampling guidance directs the quality of its outputs.
icml-2025-chip-placement-with-diffusion-.tldr: A diffusion model trained on synthetic circuits generates competitive macro placements for unseen realistic circuits without circuit-specific training.

paragraphs: This paper studies an agent that repeatedly presents a collection of items to a user and learns from the user's preference feedback. The setting captures decisions where the aim includes long-term engagement, as in recommendations or advertising. Choosing an appealing assortment now must therefore account for the future value associated with its items.

Two difficulties arise together: item values are unknown, and the number of possible assortments makes action selection challenging. The authors assume a contextual multinomial logistic preference model with linear mean utilities, while allowing a general function to approximate item value. Their algorithm, MNL-VQL, addresses efficient assortment selection while maintaining the optimism needed for its learning guarantees.

The paper establishes computational and statistical efficiency within this framework. For the special case of linear Markov decision processes with the specified preference feedback, it derives a regret lower bound and shows that MNL-VQL is near-optimal. The authors describe this as the first statistical guarantee for combinatorial reinforcement learning with preference feedback, qualified by their knowledge of prior work.
icml-2025-combinatorial-reinforcement-le.tldr: MNL-VQL learns assortments from preference feedback and achieves near-optimal regret in the studied linear-MDP special case.

paragraphs: Evaluating the safety of vision-language models requires judging harmfulness across images and text together. The authors find that existing automated evaluators can miss implicit harmful content or make inaccurate judgments. They also identify weaknesses in existing benchmarks, including ambiguous examples, low harmfulness, and limited variety in image-text combinations.

ELITE contributes both an evaluator and a benchmark built with its help. The evaluator explicitly includes a toxicity score to assess harmfulness in multimodal responses. This addresses a distinction that matters for measurement: a model can produce a detailed, convincing description of an image without that description being harmful.

The authors use the evaluator to remove ambiguous and low-quality examples from existing benchmarks and create diverse combinations of safe and unsafe images and text. Experiments show closer agreement with human evaluations than previous automated methods, along with improved benchmark quality and diversity. These contributions strengthen the tools available for identifying safety failures. Their demonstrated outcome is better evaluation, providing a basis for subsequent work on making vision-language models safer.
icml-2025-elite-enhanced-language-image-.tldr: ELITE combines a toxicity-aware evaluator with a more diverse benchmark to improve multimodal safety assessment.

paragraphs: Structure-based molecular generation aims to create ligands with desirable properties for a protein target. Learning the chemical patterns in a training dataset can produce plausible candidates, but it does not by itself offer effective control over their desired qualities. This paper focuses on steering generation toward several molecular objectives together.

The authors develop a multi-reward framework that fine-tunes a generative model for properties including binding affinity, validity, and drug-likeness. They derive direct preference optimization for a Bayesian flow network used to generate molecules. A reward-normalization scheme allows the framework to incorporate the different objectives within the same optimization process.

Experiments show that the resulting model generates more realistic ligands than the compared baselines while also achieving higher binding affinity. The authors describe this as extending the empirically observed Pareto front: their results improve the available tradeoffs among objectives rather than merely favoring one property. The work demonstrates that explicitly optimizing multiple desired attributes can improve molecular generation beyond learning the chemical distribution of the training set alone.
icml-2025-enhancing-ligand-validity-and-.tldr: Multi-reward fine-tuning improves generated ligand realism and binding affinity by jointly optimizing several molecular properties.

paragraphs: Text-to-audio systems generate sound from written descriptions, but their performance depends on many interacting design choices. This paper conducts a large empirical study of diffusion and flow-matching models to understand how training data, architecture, objectives, and sampling affect the resulting audio.

The study introduces AF-Synthetic, a dataset of high-quality synthetic captions produced by an audio-understanding model. It systematically compares choices made during model construction, training, and inference. Its sampling analysis examines quality-speed tradeoffs through Pareto curves, making the relationship between generation quality and inference cost an explicit part of the design study.

The authors combine lessons from these comparisons into ETTA. On AudioCaps and MusicCaps, it improves over baselines trained with publicly available data and remains competitive with models trained on proprietary data. They also demonstrate improved generation for complex, imaginative captions, which they identify as more challenging than current benchmarks. The contribution includes both a resulting model and empirical evidence for understanding the design decisions behind stronger text-to-audio generation.
icml-2025-etta-elucidating-the-design-sp.tldr: A systematic study of text-to-audio design choices yields ETTA, with improved benchmark results and handling of imaginative prompts.

paragraphs: Machine-learning interatomic potentials support accurate, efficient molecular dynamics simulations. In equivariant models, however, tensor-product layers can dominate computation and memory use. The paper identifies these layers as accounting for up to 75% of training time, making their implementation a substantial opportunity for accelerating these models.

FlashTP is a tensor-product library built around kernel fusion, sparse computation, and path-aggregated execution. These techniques organize the layer's computation to reduce its execution and memory overhead. The contribution targets a computational bottleneck within interatomic potentials, so its effectiveness is evaluated both at the individual-kernel level and within a complete model.

The reported kernel speedups reach 41.6 times relative to e3nn and 60.8 times relative to NVIDIA cuEquivariance. For SevenNet-l3i5, the reported inference and training speedups are 4.2 and 3.5 times, respectively, while peak memory falls by factors of 6.3 and 6.2. The distinction between kernel and model results matters: the larger local acceleration translates into substantial, separately measured gains for the evaluated model's overall execution.
icml-2025-flashtp-fused-sparsity-aware-t.tldr: FlashTP accelerates tensor-product computation and substantially reduces execution time and peak memory for the evaluated interatomic model.

paragraphs: The paper studies symmetric matrices containing both a signal and random noise, followed by a transformation applied separately to each matrix entry. The authors call the resulting object a transformed spiked Wigner matrix. Their focus is the largest eigenvalue and how its random fluctuations depend on the effective signal-to-noise ratio.

They prove that this eigenvalue exhibits a BBP-type phase transition. Above a critical effective signal-to-noise ratio, its fluctuation law converges to a Gaussian distribution. Below that critical value, it converges to the GOE Tracy-Widom distribution. Thus, changing signal strength across the threshold changes the mathematical form of the limiting randomness, not simply its magnitude.

The paper supplies precise formulas for those limiting distributions and concentration estimates in both the above-threshold and below-threshold regimes. These results characterize both the asymptotic fluctuation pattern and how tightly the largest eigenvalues concentrate. The contribution is a theoretical account of spectral behavior after an entrywise transformation, with distinct conclusions for the two stated signal-strength regimes.
icml-2025-fluctuations-of-the-largest-ei.tldr: The largest eigenvalue of a transformed spiked Wigner matrix has different limiting fluctuation laws above and below a critical signal strength.

paragraphs: Molecular design involves several tasks, from generating new candidates to modifying existing molecules toward desired goals. GenMol aims to cover these different settings with a single discrete diffusion model. Its central design uses molecular fragments as building blocks, giving the same generator a common representation for multiple kinds of design work.

The model generates SAFE sequences using bidirectional parallel decoding. This allows it to use molecular context without depending on a particular token ordering and improves sampling efficiency. For optimization, fragment remasking regenerates selected masked fragments, enabling exploration of chemical space through changes to parts of a molecule. Molecular context guidance provides an additional guidance mechanism tailored to this masked diffusion process.

GenMol substantially outperforms the previous GPT-based model on de novo and fragment-constrained generation. The authors also report state-of-the-art results for goal-directed hit generation and lead optimization. These findings support the proposed model's versatility across the evaluated tasks: the same underlying diffusion framework can generate molecules, respect fragment constraints, and support targeted molecular improvement.
icml-2025-genmol-a-drug-discovery-genera.tldr: GenMol uses fragment-based discrete diffusion to handle multiple molecular generation and optimization tasks with one model.

paragraphs: Generating motion from text becomes difficult when objects have very different skeletal structures. A model must connect language to movement while accommodating different arrangements of joints. This paper addresses both the shortage of richly annotated motion data across object categories and the challenge of using heterogeneous skeletal templates.

The authors add detailed text descriptions to Truebones Zoo, an animal-motion dataset covering more than 70 species. They also introduce rig augmentation, which creates diverse motion data while preserving consistent dynamics. These contributions expand the language supervision and skeletal variation available for learning text-controlled movement.

The modeling contribution redesigns existing motion diffusion models so they dynamically adapt to arbitrary skeletal templates. Experiments show high-fidelity motion generation from text for diverse objects, including unseen objects. Together, the data annotations, rig augmentation, and model changes address different parts of the same problem: learning how a requested movement can be expressed by objects with different structures. The findings provide evidence for extending text-to-motion synthesis across a broader range of object categories.
icml-2025-how-to-move-your-dragon-text-t.tldr: Text annotations, rig augmentation, and adaptable diffusion models enable motion generation for diverse skeletal structures, including unseen objects.

paragraphs: Larger models and more computation often improve supervised learning, but reinforcement learning can respond less reliably to scaling. Its changing training data can lead to overfitting and unstable optimization. SimbaV2 is an architecture designed to address these difficulties so that additional model capacity and computation become more useful.

The architecture combines two stabilization mechanisms. Hyperspherical normalization constrains the growth of weight and feature norms, controlling their magnitude during learning. Distributional value estimation is paired with reward scaling to maintain stable gradients when reward magnitudes vary. These mechanisms address different sources of instability within the same reinforcement-learning architecture.

Using soft actor-critic as the underlying algorithm, the authors report effective scaling with larger models and greater computation. SimbaV2 achieves state-of-the-art performance on 57 continuous-control tasks across four domains. The findings show that the proposed architecture can make scaling productive in the evaluated setting. They also connect that success to explicit control of weight, feature, and reward-related numerical behavior during optimization.
icml-2025-hyperspherical-normalization-f.tldr: SimbaV2 stabilizes reinforcement-learning optimization and scales effectively with larger models and more computation on continuous-control tasks.

paragraphs: Multinomial logistic bandits require learning from uncertain outcomes while choosing actions over time. Confidence bounds describe how much uncertainty remains in the model estimates and help guide those choices. This paper improves an online bound whose earlier form depended more heavily on both the unknown parameter's norm bound and the maximum number of outcomes.

The new confidence bound has order √(d log t) + B√d, where d is context dimension and B bounds the parameter norm. Its displayed form removes the previous explicit dependence on the outcome count and separates the time-growing term from B. The proof uses tighter self-concordant properties of the loss together with Ville's inequality.

The authors turn this bound into OFU-MNL++, a constant-time algorithm with variance-dependent optimal regret for sufficiently large horizons. They also introduce an algorithm based on maximum likelihood estimation with an anytime regret guarantee free of polynomial dependence on B. Both regret bounds track accumulated reward variance, connecting their guarantees to the uncertainty of the observed rewards.
icml-2025-improved-online-confidence-bou.tldr: Tighter online confidence bounds yield multinomial logistic bandit algorithms with improved variance-dependent regret guarantees.

paragraphs: Diffusion planners can use offline datasets to tackle tasks with long horizons and sparse rewards, yet their generated trajectories can be infeasible. This paper investigates why that happens. The authors identify inaccurate sampling guidance as the primary cause and derive a lower bound on the guidance gap to demonstrate deviation from the trajectory manifold.

Their proposed method, Local Manifold Approximation and Projection, or LoMAP, operates without additional training. It approximates a low-rank subspace from offline data and projects guided samples onto that subspace. This makes the geometry represented by the dataset directly influence sampling, addressing guidance that would otherwise move a generated trajectory away from feasible behavior.

The authors validate LoMAP on standard offline reinforcement-learning benchmarks involving difficult long-horizon planning. They also incorporate it as a standalone module into a hierarchical diffusion planner and report further performance improvements. The contribution combines a theoretical explanation of guidance-related failures with a sampling intervention that can be added to an existing planner, making it relevant to reliability as well as planning performance.
icml-2025-local-manifold-approximation-a.tldr: LoMAP projects guided diffusion samples onto a data-derived subspace to address infeasible trajectories without additional training.

paragraphs: Understanding a changing system from a few snapshots is difficult when observations are high-dimensional and collected at uneven times. Reducing dimensionality can simplify the problem, but it can also obscure dynamics and transient behavior. This paper develops a method that works with the high-dimensional observations directly.

Multi-Marginal Stochastic Flow Matching extends simulation-free score and flow matching to align data distributions at multiple observation times. Its use of measure-valued splines supports robustness to irregular timing, treating the progression as a sequence of evolving distributions. Score matching addresses overfitting in the high-dimensional space, complementing the mechanism used to connect the snapshots.

The authors validate the framework on synthetic and benchmark datasets, including gene-expression observations taken at uneven times and an image-progression task. These examples demonstrate its versatility across different kinds of high-dimensional data. The contribution is a way to combine multiple irregularly spaced observations within a single modeling framework while avoiding the dimensionality reduction that can simplify away important parts of the system's evolution.
icml-2025-multi-marginal-stochastic-flow.tldr: MMSFM models evolving high-dimensional distributions from irregularly timed snapshots without reducing dimensionality.

paragraphs: This paper studies how efficiently an algorithm can find a nearly optimal policy for an average-reward Markov decision process. Its guarantees apply to the weakly communicating setting and assume access to a generative model. The proposed procedure is model-free and combines recursive sampling with Halpern's anchored iteration.

For a target error ε, the sample and time bounds scale, up to logarithmic factors, as the number of states times the number of actions times the squared span of the bias vector, divided by ε². The bounds hold both with high probability and in expectation. The authors identify this as the best known model-free complexity, while retaining a factor equal to the bias span relative to the known lower bound.

Although the bound contains an unknown property of the problem, the algorithm does not require that property's value in advance. Its stopping rule guarantees finite termination with probability one. This separates what determines the theoretical difficulty from what the procedure needs as input. The paper also analyzes adaptations of these techniques to discounted decision processes.
icml-2025-near-optimal-sample-complexity.tldr: Anchored iteration and recursive sampling yield strong model-free complexity guarantees without requiring prior knowledge of the bias span.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning encourages matching examples to have similar embeddings and nonmatching examples to be separated. This paper studies the interaction between those goals through a unified framework based on cosine similarity. It shows that the geometry of negative pairs can influence both positive-pair alignment and the quality of the learned representation.

In full-batch training, the authors prove that perfect alignment of positive pairs is unattainable when negative-pair similarities fall below a threshold. Adding within-view negative pairs to the objective can mitigate this misalignment. The result is conditional on the stated similarity regime and identifies a tension within the training objective.

For mini-batch training, the analysis finds that smaller batches produce greater variance in negative-pair similarities and worse representations compared with full-batch training. The authors therefore introduce an auxiliary loss that reduces that variance. Experiments show improvements in small-batch settings, connecting a theoretical account of embedding geometry to a practical modification of the objective. The approach targets how negative-pair similarities are distributed, beyond merely pushing those pairs apart.
icml-2025-on-the-similarities-of-embeddi.tldr: An analysis of embedding similarities motivates a variance-reducing loss that improves contrastive learning with small batches.

paragraphs: Pruning reduces the number of active parameters in a neural network, but the resulting sparse model often loses performance. This paper approaches pruning as a search for subnetworks that are simultaneously sparse and located at flat minima. Flatness makes the optimization landscape around the chosen solution part of the pruning objective.

The authors formulate the task as constrained optimization: sparsity is an explicit constraint, and flatness is encouraged by the objective. They solve this formulation using an augmented Lagrange dual approach. A generalized projection operation extends the method, producing the two proposed pruning procedures, SAFE and SAFE+.

Evaluations cover standard image-classification and language-modeling tasks. SAFE consistently produces sparse networks with improved generalization and performs competitively against established baselines. The authors also report resilience to noisy data. These findings support combining sparsity and flatness within the pruning process as a way to improve the behavior of the resulting subnetworks. The reported gains address the performance challenge of pruning without claiming that every pruned model fully recovers its original performance.
icml-2025-safe-finding-sparse-and-flat-m.tldr: SAFE jointly targets sparsity and flatness to produce pruned networks with improved generalization and resilience to noisy data.

paragraphs: A transformer trained on easier or shorter problems can struggle when inputs become much longer or more complex. This paper investigates an iterative learning process in which a model generates solutions and then learns from its own outputs. The difficulty of the problems increases progressively while the transformer architecture remains standard.

Filtering for correct generated examples is central to the approach. Across training rounds, the authors observe exponential improvements in performance outside the original training distribution when using this filtering. The curriculum therefore depends on controlling which self-generated examples become training material as the model moves toward harder problems.

Experiments span arithmetic, string manipulation, and maze solving. One reported example extends addition from 10-digit training problems to 100-digit problems without apparent saturation. Starting from pretrained models also speeds up self-improvement on several tasks. These results show that a controlled progression from weaker to stronger capabilities can substantially expand what the evaluated models solve. The advance comes through the iterative training curriculum while preserving the simplicity of the underlying architecture.
icml-2025-self-improving-transformers-ov.tldr: Transformers trained iteratively on filtered self-generated solutions learn to solve substantially longer and harder problems.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning seeks a strong policy using an existing dataset, with out-of-distribution samples posing a central challenge. Model-based methods can augment that data using learned transitions, but they have struggled with sparse rewards and long horizons. TempDATA changes the space in which additional transitions are generated.

The method learns a geometrically structured representation of states that captures temporal distance. It draws this information from both complete trajectories and individual transitions, aiming to represent long-horizon behavior efficiently. Additional transitions are then generated in this learned representation space, giving augmentation access to temporal structure beyond the original state description.

Experiments show that TempDATA outperforms earlier offline model-based methods. It also matches or exceeds the performance of diffusion-based trajectory augmentation and goal-conditioned reinforcement learning on D4RL AntMaze, FrankaKitchen, CALVIN, and pixel-based FrankaKitchen. These are empirical comparisons across the named benchmarks. The findings support using a representation organized around temporal distance to make transition augmentation more effective for the evaluated sparse-reward and long-horizon problems.
icml-2025-temporal-distance-aware-transi.tldr: TempDATA improves offline reinforcement learning by generating transitions in a representation that captures temporal distance.

paragraphs: Models can perform poorly when deployment data differ substantially from training data. Adaptation using unlabeled test samples can help, but severe shifts remain difficult. Asking annotators for full class labels provides more supervision at a higher labeling cost. This paper introduces a setting in which annotators instead indicate whether a model's prediction is correct.

The proposed method, BiTTA, uses a small amount of this binary feedback within a dual-path optimization framework. One path adapts on uncertain samples using annotator feedback. The other uses agreement-based self-adaptation for confident predictions. Reinforcement learning balances these two sources of adaptation, combining limited external correction with information drawn from the model's own confident outputs.

Experiments report substantial accuracy improvements over state-of-the-art baselines under severe distribution shifts. The results support binary correctness judgments as useful supervision when full class annotation is costly. The contribution includes both the reduced-feedback adaptation setting and a method for deciding how to combine that feedback with self-adaptation, addressing the practical tradeoff between labeling effort and adaptation quality.
icml-2025-test-time-adaptation-with-bina.tldr: BiTTA combines a few binary correctness judgments with self-adaptation to improve accuracy under severe distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Point-cloud completion reconstructs a complete shape from an incomplete collection of points. In practical settings, an incomplete scan may have no matching complete reference. This paper studies learning from separate collections of incomplete and complete point clouds, allowing training without a paired example for every partial shape.

The proposed UOT-UPC model formulates this learning problem using unbalanced optimal transport. A neural optimal-transport model learns the mapping with neural networks. This provides a framework for connecting the incomplete and complete data collections even though their examples are not individually paired. The authors identify their work as the first use of unbalanced optimal transport for this completion setting.

Results are competitive with or better than alternatives on benchmarks containing a single object category and multiple categories. The method is especially robust when classes are imbalanced, a condition the authors identify as common in real-world unpaired completion. That finding matters because the composition of independently collected datasets can differ. The reported results support this transport-based formulation for learning completion from such unpaired collections.
icml-2025-unpaired-point-cloud-completio.tldr: UOT-UPC learns point-cloud completion from unpaired data using unbalanced optimal transport, with particular robustness to class imbalance.

paragraphs: Cooperative multi-agent systems depend on agents supporting one another, which creates opportunities for coordinated attacks. This paper investigates attacks directed at that cooperative behavior. The authors argue that traditional robustness methods in multi-agent reinforcement learning often struggle when adversaries coordinate their interference across a team.

The proposed Wolfpack attack first targets an agent and also targets the agents that assist it. Inspired by wolf hunting strategies, this structure aims to disrupt cooperation through linked pressure on the initial target and its support. The paper pairs this attack with Wolfpack-Adversarial Learning for MARL, or WALL, which trains policies to defend against it by encouraging collaboration across the system.

Experiments show a severe impact from the Wolfpack attack and substantial robustness improvements from WALL. The attack and defense therefore serve complementary purposes: one exposes weaknesses in cooperative behavior, and the other trains collaboration to withstand the proposed threat. The findings support treating robustness as a property of the interacting team, with the reported defense gains established against the evaluated Wolfpack attack.
icml-2025-wolfpack-adversarial-attack-fo.tldr: Wolfpack attacks an agent and its helpers, while WALL trains team-wide collaboration to improve robustness against that attack.
